results.title: Residue class
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For integers $r$ and $m$, the residue class $r(m)$ is the set $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : x \equiv r \pmod{m}\} = \{r + k m : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$.

results.title: Class transposition of two residue classes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For integers $r_1, m_1, r_2, m_2$, write $r_1(m_1) = r_1 + m_1\mathbb{Z}$ and $r_2(m_2) = r_2 + m_2\mathbb{Z}$ for the residue classes. A permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is the class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1), r_2(m_2)}$ when $0 \le r_1 < m_1$ and $0 \le r_2 < m_2$, the residue classes $r_1(m_1)$ and $r_2(m_2)$ are disjoint, $\sigma$ interchanges $r_1 + k m_1$ and $r_2 + k m_2$ for every integer $k$, and…

results.title: Class transpositions of the integers
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A permutation $\sigma$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a class transposition when it is the class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1), r_2(m_2)}$ for some integers $r_1, m_1, r_2, m_2$.

results.title: Claim of Kourovka Problem 18.48
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Only finitely many positive integers occur as orders of products $\sigma\tau$ of two class transpositions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ of $\mathbb{Z}$.

results.title: Products of two class transpositions have only finitely many orders
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The claim of Kourovka Problem 18.48 holds: the set of positive integers $k$ such that $\sigma\tau$ has order $k$ for some class transpositions $\sigma$ and $\tau$ of $\mathbb{Z}$ is finite.

results.title: Lattice terms
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: Lattice terms in the variables $x_0, x_1, x_2, \dots$ are built inductively: each variable $x_n$ is a term, and for terms $s$ and $t$ their join $s \vee t$ and their meet $s \wedge t$ are terms.

results.title: Evaluation of lattice terms
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a lattice and $v$ an assignment of an element $v(n)$ of $L$ to each variable $x_n$. The value of a lattice term under $v$ is defined by recursion on the term: the variable $x_n$ has value $v(n)$, and a join $s \vee t$ or meet $s \wedge t$ has as value the join or meet in $L$ of the values of $s$ and $t$.

results.title: Blocks of a group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A subset $X$ of a group $G$ is a block if it is empty or a coset $gN$ of a normal subgroup $N$ of $G$ (Kourovka Notebook, Archive 9.62). Ordered by inclusion, the blocks of $G$ form the block lattice $C(G)$.

results.title: Join in the block lattice
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For subsets $X$ and $Y$ of a group $G$, their block join is the intersection of all blocks of $G$ that contain $X \cup Y$. Since blocks are closed under intersections and $G$ itself is a block, this is the smallest block containing $X \cup Y$; for blocks $X$ and $Y$ it is their join in the block lattice of $G$.

results.title: Evaluation of lattice terms in the block lattice
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a group and $v$ an assignment of a subset $v(n)$ of $G$ to each variable $x_n$. The value of a lattice term under $v$ is defined by recursion on the term: the variable $x_n$ has value $v(n)$, a meet $s \wedge t$ has as value the intersection of the values of $s$ and $t$, and a join $s \vee t$ has as value the block join of the values of $s$ and $t$, the intersection of all blocks of $G$ containing their…

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The block lattices of finite groups do not generate the variety of all lattices: there are lattice terms $p$ and $q$ such that $p$ and $q$ take the same value in the block lattice of every finite group $G$ under every assignment of blocks of $G$ to the variables, but take different values in some lattice $L$ under some assignment of elements of $L$ to the variables. results.title: Schur's lemma, dimension form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $k$ an algebraically closed field, and $\rho$, $\sigma$ irreducible representations of $G$ on finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces. Then the space $\operatorname{Hom}_G(\rho, \sigma)$ of intertwining maps from $\rho$ to $\sigma$ has dimension $1$ over $k$ if $\sigma$ and $\rho$ are equivalent, and dimension $0$ otherwise.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a finite group, $k$ an algebraically closed field, and $(\rho_i)_{i \in I}$ a family, indexed by a finite set $I$, of irreducible representations of $G$ on finite-dimensional $k$-vector spaces that are pairwise non-equivalent: $\rho_i$ and $\rho_j$ are not equivalent whenever $i \ne j$. results.title: The range of a bounded operator as a set
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E'$ and $F'$ be Hilbert spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $S : E' \to F'$ be a bounded linear operator. The set of values of $S$ equals the underlying set of the range of $S$ regarded as a linear subspace of $F'$.

results.title: Restriction to the orthogonal complement of the kernel keeps the range
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ be a Hilbert space and $F$ an inner product space over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the restriction of $T$ to the orthogonal complement $(\ker T)^\perp$ of its kernel has the same range as $T$: every value $T x$ is attained at the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto $(\ker T)^\perp$, since the difference lies in…

results.title: Restriction to the orthogonal complement of the kernel is injective
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ and $F$ be inner product spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear operator. Then the restriction of $T$ to the orthogonal complement $(\ker T)^\perp$ of its kernel is injective: a vector lying in both $\ker T$ and $(\ker T)^\perp$ is zero.

results.title: Closed range passes to the adjoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ and $F$ be Hilbert spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear operator with adjoint $T^\dagger$. If the range of $T$ is closed in $F$, then the range of $T^\dagger$ is closed in $E$.

results.title: Closed range theorem for adjoints
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $E$ and $F$ be Hilbert spaces over $\mathbb{K}$, where $\mathbb{K}$ is $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$, and let $T : E \to F$ be a bounded linear operator with adjoint $T^\dagger$. Then the range of $T$ is closed in $F$ if and only if the range of $T^\dagger$ is closed in $E$.

results.title: Closed range from a Fredholm $T^*T$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Closed range from a Fredholm $T^*T$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $T : X \to Y$ be a bounded linear operator with Hilbert space adjoint $T^* : Y \to X$. If $T^*T : X \to X$ is a Fredholm operator, then the range of $T$ is closed in $Y$.

results.title: Closed range passes to the Hilbert space adjoint
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $X$ and $Y$ be complex Hilbert spaces and let $A : X \to Y$ be a bounded linear operator with Hilbert space adjoint $A^* : Y \to X$. If the range of $A$ is closed in $Y$, then the range of $A^*$ is closed in $X$.

results.title: Uniform $\ell^1$ lower bound
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $E$ be a normed space over $\mathbb{K} = \mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. A sequence $(y_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ in $E$ has a uniform $\ell^1$ lower bound when there is a real $c > 0$ such that $\|\sum_i a_i y_i\| \ge c \sum_i |a_i|$ for every finitely supported sequence $(a_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ of scalars in $\mathbb{K}$, both sums running over the finitely many $i$ with $a_i \ne 0$.

results.caption: Theorem

Then there is a strictly increasing $\varphi : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that either the subsequence $(x_{\varphi(n)})_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ is weakly Cauchy, that is, for every continuous linear functional $f : E \to \mathbb{K}$ and every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$…

results.title: Modulus of continuity
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a function $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, real numbers $a$ and $b$, and a scale $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$, the modulus of continuity of $f$ on $[a, b]$ at scale $\eta$ is

results.title: The set defining the modulus of continuity is bounded above
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a, b]$. Then for every $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$ the set $\{|f(x) - f(y)| : x, y \in [a, b],\ |x - y| \le \eta\}$ is bounded above.

results.title: The modulus of continuity bounds increments
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a, b]$, let $\eta \in \mathbb{R}$, and let $\omega_f(\eta)$ be the modulus of continuity of $f$ on $[a, b]$ at scale $\eta$. For all $x, y \in [a, b]$ with $|x - y| \le \eta$, we have $|f(x) - f(y)| \le \omega_f(\eta)$.

results.title: Nonnegativity of the modulus of continuity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a \le b$ and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a, b]$. For every $\eta \ge 0$, the modulus of continuity $\omega_f(\eta)$ of $f$ on $[a, b]$ at scale $\eta$ satisfies $0 \le \omega_f(\eta)$.

results.title: Monotonicity of the modulus of continuity
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a \le b$, let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a, b]$, and write $\omega_f(\eta)$ for the modulus of continuity of $f$ on $[a, b]$ at scale $\eta$. If $0 \le \eta_1 \le \eta_2$, then $\omega_f(\eta_1) \le \omega_f(\eta_2)$.

results.title: Theorem I (Modulus of continuity vanishes)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a \le b$ and let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a, b]$. Then the modulus of continuity $\omega_f(\eta)$ of $f$ on $[a, b]$ tends to $0$ as $\eta \to 0^+$.

results.title: Terms of Ramanujan's factorial series
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real number $x$ and a natural number $j$, the $j$-th term of Ramanujan's factorial series is $(-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$, read as $0$ when the denominator vanishes.

results.title: Ramanujan's factorial series
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a real number $x$, $C(x)$ is the sum $\sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ of Ramanujan's factorial series, where a term is read as $0$ when its denominator vanishes and the sum is taken to be $0$ when the series is not summable.

results.title: Convergence of Ramanujan's factorial series
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every real $x > 0$, the series $\sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ is summable.

results.title: Recursion for the terms of Ramanujan's factorial series
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Write $c_j(x) = (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ for the $j$-th term of Ramanujan's factorial series, with division by $0$ read as $0$. For every real $x$ and every natural number $j$, $c_{j+1}(x) = -\frac{1}{x + 1} \, c_j(x + 1)$.

results.title: Functional equation of Ramanujan's factorial series
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C(x) = \sum_{j \ge 0} (-1)^j / ((x + 1)(x + 2) \cdots (x + j + 1))$ be Ramanujan's factorial series. For every real $x > 0$, $C(x) = \frac{1}{x + 1} - \frac{C(x + 1)}{x + 1}$.

results.title: Summability of Ramanujan's factorial series in a sector, for every $x$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be a complex number and let $\varepsilon > 0$ be a real number. Then there is a real number $R$ such that for every complex number $z$ with $|z| \ge R$ whose principal argument satisfies $-\pi + \varepsilon \le \arg z \le \pi - \varepsilon$, the series $\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} \frac{(-1)^j x^{j+1}}{(z+1)(z+2)\cdots(z+j+1)}$ is summable.

results.title: Convolution powers of a Gaussian are Gaussian
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The convolution power of a Gaussian is Gaussian with the mean and the variance multiplied by `n`: the law of the sum of `n` i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` variables is `N(nμ, nv)`.

results.title: Stable distribution of a given index
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Indexed stability fixes the positive-n dilation to `n^(1/α)` and allows arbitrary centering. Degenerate Dirac identities may satisfy several indices.

results.title: Dirac measures are stable of every index
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A Dirac law satisfies the fixed-dilation identity at every admissible index. These are degenerate rescaling identities, with centering `na - n^(1/α)a`.

results.title: Gaussian measures are stable of index 2
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every real Gaussian measure is stable of index `2`: the sum of `n` i.i.d. `N(μ, v)` variables is `N(nμ, nv)`, which is the pushforward of `N(μ, v)` under `x ↦ √n · x + (n - √n) μ`.

results.title: Nondegenerate Gaussian is not stable of index 1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nondegenerate Gaussian cannot have fixed stability index one. The n=4 convolution variance is `4v`, while every such affine dilation has variance `16v`.

results.title: Nondegenerate measure on the real line
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A measure `μ` on `ℝ` is *nondegenerate* if it is not a point mass `δ_a` for any `a`.

results.title: Gaussian with nonzero variance is nondegenerate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A Gaussian with nonzero variance is nondegenerate: it gives mass `0` to every singleton, while `δ_a` gives mass `1` to `{a}`.

results.title: Dirac measure is degenerate
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A Dirac measure is degenerate, by definition.

results.title: Domain of attraction
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The probability measure `μ` is *in the domain of attraction* of `G` if there exist sequences of normalizing constants `a n > 0` and centering constants `b n` such that the law of `(S_n - b n) / a n` (where `S_n` has law `μ^{*n}`) converges weakly to `G`, expressed here as integration against arbitrary bounded continuous functions.

results.title: Stable law lies in its own domain of attraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A stable law is a normalized weak limit of its own convolution powers. The positive-n inverse affine identity is exact; order zero uses normalizer one.

results.title: Domain of attraction of a given index
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Indexed attraction requires a nondegenerate stable limit of that index. The general normalized weak-limit relation alone does not assign an index.

results.title: Dirac measure lies in its own domain of attraction
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Dirac measure is in its own domain of attraction: with `a n = 1` and `b n = (n - 1) a`, the normalized law of `S_n` is `δ_a` for every `n`.

results.title: Complement of a Boolean vector
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The complement of a Boolean vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$ is the vector $\bar x \in \{0,1\}^n$ obtained by negating every coordinate: $\bar x_i = \lnot x_i$ for every $i < n$.

results.title: Dual of a Boolean function
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, its dual is the Boolean function $f^\star \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ given by $f^\star(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$, where $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.

results.title: Self-dual monotone Boolean functions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$ is self-dual monotone when it is monotone, that is, $f(x) \le f(y)$ for all $x, y \in \{0,1\}^n$ with $x_i \le y_i$ for every $i < n$, and it equals its dual, that is, $f = f^\star$, where $f^\star(x) = \lnot f(\bar x)$ and $\bar x$ is the coordinatewise complement of $x$.

results.title: Complementation of Boolean vectors is an involution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$ and every Boolean vector $x \in \{0,1\}^n$, writing $\bar x$ for the coordinatewise complement of $x$, we have $\bar{\bar x} = x$.

results.title: Duality of Boolean functions is an involution
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$ and every Boolean function $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \{0,1\}$, writing $f^\star$ for the dual of $f$, we have $(f^\star)^\star = f$.

results.title: Coordinate projections are self-dual monotone
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every $n$ and every index $i < n$, the projection $x \mapsto x_i$ on $\{0,1\}^n$ is a self-dual monotone Boolean function.

results.title: Concatenation at the all-false input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $n$ and $k$ and a finite list $W = (W_0, \dots, W_{m-1})$ of Boolean functions on $n$ variables, the concatenation of $W$ on $n + k$ variables takes the value $W_0(\mathrm{false}, \dots, \mathrm{false})$ at the all-false input when $W$ is nonempty, and the value false when $W$ is empty.

results.title: Currying monotone Boolean functions (Lemma 1)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a natural number $m$, let $D_m$ be the poset of monotone Boolean functions $\{0,1\}^m \to \{0,1\}$, where $0 < 1$, inputs are ordered coordinatewise and functions are ordered pointwise. Then for all natural numbers $n$ and $k$, $D_{n+k}$ is order-isomorphic to the poset of monotone maps $\{0,1\}^k \to D_n$, ordered pointwise.

results.title: Duality reverses order and exchanges joins and meets
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ and $g$ be monotone Boolean functions on $n$ variables, ordered pointwise, with duals $f^*$ and $g^*$. If $f \le g$ then $g^* \le f^*$. Moreover $(f \lor g)^* = f^* \land g^*$ and $(f \land g)^* = f^* \lor g^*$, where $\lor$ and $\land$ are pointwise disjunction and conjunction.

results.title: Permuting variables preserves monotonicity, duals and self-duality
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $f$ be a Boolean function on $n$ variables, let $\pi$ be a permutation of the $n$ coordinates, and let $f^\pi$ be the function $x \mapsto f(x \circ \pi)$. If $f$ is monotone, then $f^\pi$ is monotone and $(f^*)^\pi = (f^\pi)^*$, where $f^*$ is the dual of $f$. If $f$ is self-dual monotone, then so is $f^\pi$.

results.summary: Let $n \ge 1$ and let $\mathcal U$ be a maximal intersecting family of subsets of $X = \{0, \dots, n-1\}$: any two members of $\mathcal U$, not necessarily distinct, have nonempty intersection, and no family of subsets of $X$ strictly containing $\mathcal U$ has this property. results.title: Weakly $p$-small families
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $X$ be a finite set, $p \in [0, 1]$, and $\mathcal F$ a family of subsets of $X$. Then $\mathcal F$ is weakly $p$-small if there is a function $g$ from subsets of $X$ to the nonnegative reals such that $\sum_{S \subseteq T} g(S) \ge 1$ for every $T \in \mathcal F$ and $\sum_{S \subseteq X} g(S)\, p^{|S|} \le 1/2$.

results.title: The threshold $p_c(\mathcal F)$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a set $X$ and $p \in [0, 1]$, let $\mu_p$ be the $p$-biased product measure on subsets of $X$, under which each element of $X$ lies in the random subset independently with probability $p$. For a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of $X$, $p_c(\mathcal F)$ is some $p \in [0, 1]$ with $\mu_p(\mathcal F) = 1/2$ if such a $p$ exists, and $0$ otherwise.

results.title: The fractional expectation-threshold $q_f(\mathcal F)$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of a finite set $X$, $q_f(\mathcal F)$ is the supremum, in $[0, 1]$, of the set of all $p \in [0, 1]$ such that $\mathcal F$ is weakly $p$-small; it is $0$ if there is no such $p$.

results.title: Size of a largest minimal element, $\ell(\mathcal F)$
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a family $\mathcal F$ of subsets of a set $X$, $\ell(\mathcal F)$ is the largest cardinality of a minimal element of $\mathcal F$ (minimal with respect to inclusion), a natural number.

The model domain is `θ > 0` and `x ∈ (0, 1)`; at…

results.title: Closed form of the Poisson random field density with selection
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The Poisson-random-field density with selection, explicitly: `θ (1 - e^{-2σ(1 - x)}) / ((1 - e^{-2σ}) x (1 - x))` for `σ ≠ 0`.

results.title: Neutral Poisson random field density
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The neutral Poisson-random-field density is `θ / x` (for `x ≠ 1`).

results.title: The neutral density from the Green's function
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A new neutral mutation enters at a small frequency `p`; with mutations arriving at rate `θ / (2p)` per unit time (so that the mutational input of frequency is `θ / 2`), the expected sojourn density at `x ≥ p` is `θ / (2p) · G(p, x) = θ / x`, the neutral Poisson-random-field density.

results.title: Stationary forward equation (Sawyer–Hartl 1992)
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On `(0, 1)` the weighted density `F(x) = x (1 - x) φ(x)` of the Poisson-random-field density solves the stationary Fokker–Planck equation `½ F'' - σ F' = 0` of the Wright–Fisher diffusion with genic selection `σ` (the forward equation `½ (x (1 - x) φ)'' - (σ x (1 - x) φ)' = 0`).

results.title: Probability current
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: On `(0, 1)` the current `J = σ F - F' / 2` of the stationary forward equation, for the weighted density `F(x) = x (1 - x) φ(x)`, is the constant `θ · u_σ'(0) / 2` (`u_σ'(0) = kimuraSlope σ = 2σ / (1 - e^{-2σ})`, and `1` for `σ = 0`), so `J = θ σ / (1 - e^{-2σ})`, and `J = θ / 2` in the neutral case: the mutational input of frequency at `0`, carried through `(0, 1)` to fixation at `1`.

results.title: Boundary normalization at `0`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: As `x → 0⁺` the weighted density `x (1 - x) φ(x)` tends to `θ`. (This is not the probability current, which is `current_prfDensity`.)

results.title: Boundary normalization at `1`
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: As `x → 1⁻` the weighted density `x (1 - x) φ(x)` tends to `0`.

results.title: ODE characterization of the Poisson-random-field density
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let `θ ≠ 0` and let `φ` be a density on `(0, 1)` whose weighted density `x (1 - x) φ(x)` extends to a function `F` continuous on `[0, 1]`, twice differentiable on `(0, 1)`, solving the stationary forward equation `½ F'' - σ F' = 0` there, with boundary normalizations `F(0) = θ` and `F(1) = 0`. Then `φ` is the Sawyer–Hartl density on `(0, 1)`.

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With `σ = 0`, for the segregating classes `1 ≤ i < n` the expected number of sites with `i` derived copies in a sample of `n` is `θ / i`.

results.summary: With `σ = 0` the expected number of sites at which all `n ≥ 1` sampled copies carry the derived allele is `θ / n`. These sites are monomorphic in the sample, so this is not a class of the site-frequency spectrum.
